project_1_short: Storage, Processing, and Transmission of Information on Millions of Shipments.
project_1_long: A high-load backend that stores and processes over 3 million different shipments. It is used by everyone from managers to regular employees, who have varying levels of access rights. Data is retrieved, updated, and modified not only by warehouse staff but also via the Ozon API. Webhooks have been created for the CodeReader service, which allows for quick and convenient barcode scanning.
project_2_short: A ready-to-use service for learning English through movies and TV shows on YouTube, along with various games to increase engagement.
project_2_long: Writing new features, fixing bugs, and deploying updates to the server for an English-learning service based on YouTube videos. The following features were implemented: multithreaded video processing, transcription handling, and various games designed to make our service more appealing to customers.
project_3_short: A simple service for viewing video content.
project_3_long: A personal project for viewing various video content. The frontend is built with Svelte 5, which communicates with the FastAPI backend via a REST API. It features a user system, video playback history tracking, and a search engine. All videos are stored in S3 in a special format that allows content to be delivered to thousands of users simultaneously. I created this format using automated workers that convert the source video with FFmpeg, transcoding it into various resolutions (360, 720, 1080) and a modern codec. The website features a video player built from scratch that automatically analyzes user data to select the optimal video quality.

project_4_long: A high-load backend that stores and processes over million different shipments. After consulting with our clients from China, we selected the best logistics solution for them for shipments between China and Russia.
project_5_short: Automatic analysis and processing of purchase bonuses

project_6_title: Telegram bot for sellers on Wildberries
project_6_short: All kinds of analytics and calculators
project_6_long: It allows you to track various metrics, receive notifications when testing changes to various variables in the product card, and work with the Wildberries API. It also encrypts user data, such as API keys, for security.
project_7_title: Schedule Bot for Telegram, VK, and MAX
project_7_short: Multi-platform bot that helps students find their college schedule and notifies them when it changes.
project_7_long: Developed a multi-platform schedule bot for Telegram, VK, and MAX. Implemented automatic analysis of the college website, collection of all data, and its further processing. Users can quickly find their college schedule and receive notifications about schedule changes. Implemented a unified database layer for all messengers, a queue-based system for broadcasts and alerts, and concurrent request handling.

hash_algo_sha256_desc: The primary cryptographic hash for SSL/TLS certificates, Git commits, and Bitcoin mining. Delivers the ideal trade-off between performance and collision resistance.
hash_algo_sha512_desc: Outputs a 512-bit digest (128 hex chars). Optimized for 64-bit CPU architectures, frequently running faster than SHA-256 while offering maximum post-quantum security margin.
hash_algo_sha384_desc: Truncated version of SHA-512 with a unique initial vector. Commonly required in high-compliance US Federal/Suite B cipher suites and TLS 1.3.
hash_algo_md5_desc: Lightweight 128-bit checksum. Cryptographically broken with instant collision vulnerabilities; suitable only for basic non-adversarial file integrity checks.
hash_algo_sha1_desc: A 160-bit digest formerly standard in Git and older TLS. Broken via collision attacks (SHAttered, 2017). Avoid in new cryptographic protocols.
hash_algo_keccak256_desc: The raw Keccak-256 specification with 0x01 padding. The core hashing algorithm of the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM), Solidity contracts, and address derivation.
hash_algo_sha3_256_desc: Standardized by NIST with 0x06 domain padding. Built on Keccak sponge construction, making it completely immune to length extension attacks.
hash_algo_sha3_512_desc: The highest-security SHA-3 variant. Well-suited for cryptographic research and long-term data security against quantum brute-force vectors.
hash_algo_sha3_384_desc: Intermediate 384-bit SHA-3 digest, structurally matched with 192-bit and 256-bit symmetric encryption standards.
hash_algo_sha3_224_desc: Compact SHA-3 digest engineered to replace legacy 224-bit hashes like SHA-224.
hash_algo_blake2b_desc: 64-bit optimized hash faster than MD5 and SHA-1 while matching SHA-3 security. Extensively utilized in WireGuard VPN, Argon2, and IPFS.
hash_algo_blake2b_256_desc: BLAKE2b configured to produce a compact 256-bit digest, providing high throughput on 64-bit systems with minimal digest length.
hash_algo_blake2s_desc: 32-bit architecture variant optimized for microcontrollers, embedded IoT hardware, and lightweight cryptographic operations.
hash_algo_xxhash32_desc: Extremely fast non-cryptographic hash algorithm executing near RAM speed limits. Provides outstanding avalanche effect and collision avoidance for in-memory indexing.
hash_algo_murmur3_128_desc: High-throughput 128-bit hash developed by Austin Appleby. Universally deployed in databases (Cassandra), Bloom filters, and large-scale data systems.
hash_algo_murmur3_32_desc: Standard 32-bit MurmurHash3. Ideal for in-memory hash maps, cache key distribution, and quick data bucketing.
hash_algo_murmur2_64_desc: 64-bit MurmurHash2 variant optimized for 64-bit architectures, frequently leveraged in high-load server key distribution.
hash_algo_murmur2_32_desc: 32-bit MurmurHash2 algorithm widely found in legacy data frameworks, search engines, and real-time metrics pipelines.
hash_algo_crc32_desc: Cyclic Redundancy Check (32-bit). Specifically designed to detect accidental transmission or storage errors in network packets (Ethernet), ZIP archives, and PNG images.
hash_algo_crc64_desc: 64-bit Cyclic Redundancy Check providing a substantially lower accidental collision probability for big file validation and storage blocks.
hash_algo_adler32_desc: Rolling checksum invented by Mark Adler. Computes faster than CRC-32 in pure software and is the core checksum standard in zlib compression.
hash_algo_streebog256_desc: Russian cryptographic hash standard (GOST R 34.11-2012, 256-bit). Developed by TC 26 using an AES-like substitution-permutation network (SPN).
hash_algo_streebog512_desc: 512-bit variant of GOST R 34.11-2012 (Streebog). Standardized for national digital signature verification and official cryptographic documents.
hash_algo_whirlpool_desc: 512-bit hash function designed by Vincent Rijmen and Paulo Barreto. Employs a heavily modified AES cipher square matrix (MDS matrix) for diffusion.
hash_algo_ripemd160_desc: 160-bit European cryptographic standard. Essential to Bitcoin address generation where it is combined with SHA-256 (HASH160).
hash_guide_intro: Hash functions map arbitrary amounts of data to fixed-size outputs. They are categorized into cryptographic hashes (irreversible, collision-resistant), fast non-cryptographic hashes (optimized for hash table lookups and Bloom filters), and cyclic checksums (designed for error detection in transmission).
hash_faq_q1: What is the difference between Keccak-256 and SHA3-256?
hash_faq_a1: Although Keccak won the NIST hash competition to become SHA-3, NIST changed the domain separation padding byte from 0x01 to 0x06 in the final standard. Ethereum launched prior to this update and kept the original Keccak-256. Consequently, their hashes for the same text do not match.
hash_faq_q2: What is the difference between cryptographic and non-cryptographic hashes?
hash_faq_a2: Cryptographic hashes (SHA-256, BLAKE2, Streebog) are designed to be mathematically irreversible and collision-resistant against malicious attackers. Non-cryptographic hashes (xxHash, MurmurHash) prioritize raw throughput for hash tables and Bloom filters, making them fast but vulnerable to intentional collision attacks.
hash_faq_q3: Can a cryptographic hash be decrypted or reversed?
hash_faq_a3: No. A hash is a one-way digest, not symmetric or asymmetric encryption. Information is irreversibly reduced. However, predictable or short inputs can be matched using precomputed rainbow tables or dictionary attacks.
hash_faq_q4: Which hash function should I use for user passwords?
hash_faq_a4: Never use raw fast hashes like SHA-256, SHA-512, or MD5 alone for passwords. Modern GPUs calculate billions of hashes per second. Always employ memory-hard key derivation functions such as Argon2id, bcrypt, or scrypt.
hash_faq_q5: When should I choose CRC32 or Adler-32 instead of SHA-256?
hash_faq_a5: CRC-32 and Adler-32 are error-detecting checksums, not secure hashes. Use them when you need to verify network packet integrity, compressed archives (ZIP/zlib), or stream transfer errors with minimal CPU overhead.
hash_faq_a6: xxHash is an exceptionally fast non-cryptographic algorithm that operates at the maximum bandwidth limits of system RAM while achieving near-perfect randomness. It is the gold standard for in-memory indexing, game engines, and databases.
hash_faq_a7: Streebog is the national cryptographic hash function of the Russian Federation. It replaced the outdated GOST R 34.11-94 and uses an internal structure based on the AES/Kuznyechik SPN design.
hash_faq_q8: Why does BLAKE2b have both 256-bit and 512-bit versions?
hash_faq_a8: BLAKE2b is naturally optimized for 64-bit processors using 64-bit words, internally computing a 512-bit state. It can be safely truncated to 256 bits, offering 64-bit speed while producing a smaller digest.
hash_faq_q9: Are my strings or files uploaded to your server?
hash_faq_a9: No. All computations are performed locally in your browser using WebAssembly and Web Crypto API modules. No data is transmitted across the internet.
hash_faq_a10: The avalanche effect is a fundamental property where a modification of a single bit in the input causes approximately 50% of the bits in the resulting hash to flip randomly.

encode_fmt_base64_desc: Base64 (RFC 4648) encodes every 3 bytes into 4 ASCII characters from A–Z a–z 0–9 + /. Padding with = keeps the length a multiple of 4. Used in MIME email, data URIs, JWT, Kubernetes secrets and more.
encode_fmt_base64url_desc: URL-safe variant: + → -, / → _, no padding. Used in JWT, OAuth and anywhere a token must survive being embedded in a URL or filename.
encode_fmt_base32_desc: Uses A–Z 2–7. Case-insensitive, so it is preferred for TOTP secrets and anywhere a human has to type the value.
encode_fmt_hex_desc: Each byte is represented by two hexadecimal characters. The most common representation for hashes, MACs and raw binary data in a readable form.
encode_fmt_url_desc: Escapes reserved characters as %XX. Required for query parameters, path segments and form data (encodeURIComponent / decodeURIComponent).
encode_fmt_html_desc: Escapes & < > " ' to prevent XSS and to safely render user-provided content inside HTML. Supports named and numeric entities.
encode_fmt_rot13_desc: A trivial Caesar shift by 13 — its own inverse. Useful for hiding spoilers and puzzles, not for security.
encode_fmt_binary_desc: Each byte as 8 bits, space-separated. Handy for teaching, bitwise debugging and low-level protocols.
encode_fmt_ascii_desc: Each byte as a decimal code point (0–255). Useful for legacy protocols and character set debugging.
encode_faq_a1: Base64 is a binary-to-text encoding that represents arbitrary bytes using 64 printable ASCII characters (A–Z, a–z, 0–9, +, /). It is used to embed binary data in JSON, XML, email (MIME) and data URIs.
encode_faq_q2: What is the difference between Base64 and Base64 URL?
encode_faq_a2: Base64 URL replaces '+' with '-' and '/' with '_' and omits padding '='. It is safe to use in URLs and filenames, e.g. in JWTs.
encode_faq_q3: How do I decode a hex string?
encode_faq_a3: Paste the hex string into the input, select 'Hex' and press Decode. Every two hex characters represent one byte.
encode_faq_a4: No. Encoding and decoding happen entirely in your browser.

uuid_versions_intro: A UUID (Universally Unique Identifier) is a 128-bit value. The standard specifies versions 1 through 8, each tailored for specific architectural requirements.
uuid_v1_desc: Constructed from a 60-bit timestamp counting 100-nanosecond intervals since the Gregorian calendar reform (1582), a clock sequence, and the device's 48-bit MAC address.
uuid_v3_v5_desc: Deterministic identifiers computed by hashing a namespace UUID and an input name. v3 uses MD5, while v5 uses SHA-1. Identical inputs always yield the identical UUID.
uuid_v4_desc: Purely random UUID. 122 out of 128 bits are generated using cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generators (CSPRNG), leaving 6 bits for version and variant.
uuid_v7_desc: The modern RFC 9562 standard (2024). Features a 48-bit millisecond Unix timestamp prefix followed by random bits, delivering superior B-Tree database locality.
uuid_v6_desc: A field-reordered variation of UUID v1 designed to store timestamp bits in big-endian order for legacy sorting systems.
uuid_v8_desc: An RFC 9562 reserved specification allowing custom or experimental vendor-specific layouts while retaining standard variant and version bits.
uuid_minecraft_info: In Minecraft Java Edition, paid accounts receive an online UUID v4 from Mojang authorization servers. In offline (LAN or non-authenticated) environments, the client and server derive a deterministic UUID v3 from 'OfflinePlayer:<Username>'. Furthermore, Minecraft version 1.16 and newer stores entity UUIDs in NBT as an array of four 32-bit signed integers: [I; int1, int2, int3, int4].
uuid_faq_q1: What is the key advantage of UUID v7 over UUID v4?
uuid_faq_a1: UUID v4 is entirely random, which causes severe B-Tree page fragmentation and random I/O write penalties in relational databases. UUID v7 embeds a millisecond-precision Unix timestamp in its initial 48 bits, allowing newly inserted rows to be appended sequentially.
uuid_faq_q2: What are the odds of a UUID v4 collision?
uuid_faq_a2: The total number of possible UUID v4 values is 2¹²² (approx. 5.3 × 10³⁶). Even generating one billion UUIDs per second for 100 consecutive years yields an astronomically negligible collision probability.
uuid_faq_q3: What does the Minecraft NBT [I; ...] format represent?
uuid_faq_a3: Beginning in Minecraft 1.16, the game serializes 128-bit UUIDs as four 32-bit signed integers in NBT files, optimizing entity lookup speeds and reducing serialization overhead.
uuid_faq_q4: What is the Single Integer Value in the decoder output?
uuid_faq_a4: A UUID is fundamentally an unsigned 128-bit binary number. When interpreted as a big-endian integer, it represents a single BigInt value up to 2¹²⁸ - 1, which is often used in mathematical models and binary network protocols.
uuid_faq_q5: Does UUID v1 leak hardware information?
uuid_faq_a5: Original implementations of v1 utilized the physical network card MAC address. Modern standards (and our browser implementation) use cryptographically pseudo-random node bytes with the local multicast bit asserted to guarantee anonymity.

hmac_guide_intro: HMAC (Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code) is a specific type of message authentication code involving a cryptographic hash function in combination with a secret key. It guarantees both data integrity and authenticity: an attacker without the secret key cannot forge a valid tag.
hmac_faq_q1: What is HMAC and why is it needed?
hmac_faq_a1: HMAC verifies that a received message is authentic and has not been altered in transit. Unlike a raw hash, computing an HMAC requires a shared secret key.
hmac_faq_q2: What is the difference between SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA256?
hmac_faq_a2: SHA-256 is an unkeyed hash that anyone can compute for any text. HMAC-SHA256 uses nested hashing with inner (ipad) and outer (opad) key paddings, making it mathematically impossible to forge without knowing the secret key.
hmac_faq_q3: Which HMAC algorithm should I choose for a new system?
hmac_faq_a3: HMAC-SHA-256 is the standard choice for modern software (JWT HS256, API webhooks). For higher security requirements, choose HMAC-SHA-512 or HMAC-SHA3-256. Use HMAC-SHA-1 or HMAC-MD5 only when required for backward compatibility.
hmac_faq_q4: How long should the secret key be?
hmac_faq_a4: The secret key should be at least as long as the output size of the chosen hash function. For HMAC-SHA256, use at least 32 cryptographically random bytes (256 bits). Keys longer than the hash block size are pre-hashed automatically.
hmac_faq_q5: Does HMAC prevent Length Extension attacks?
hmac_faq_a5: Yes. Naive construction H(key || message) is vulnerable to length extension attacks in Merkle-Damgård hashes. HMAC's double-hash formula H(K ⊕ opad || H(K ⊕ ipad || message)) completely neutralizes this vector.
hmac_faq_q6: Where is HMAC used in modern protocols?
hmac_faq_a6: JSON Web Tokens (JWT HS256/HS384/HS512), AWS Signature V4, Stripe and GitHub webhook signatures, TOTP/HOTP 2-factor authentication, IPsec, and TLS 1.3 PRF.
hmac_faq_a7: An authentication code built on top of the Russian national cryptographic hash standard GOST R 34.11-2012 (Streebog). Widely required in government IT systems across Russia and the EAEU.
hmac_faq_q8: Where is the Chinese HMAC-SM3 standard used?
hmac_faq_a8: SM3 is the official national standard of China (GB/T 32918), mandatory for commercial cryptography, UnionPay financial transactions, and compliance in China.
hmac_faq_q9: Are my secret keys or messages transmitted to a server?
hmac_faq_a9: No. All computations are executed 100% locally in your browser using JavaScript and WebAssembly. No sensitive credentials or payloads ever leave your device.

cipher_desc_chacha: High-throughput stream cipher by Daniel J. Bernstein (RFC 8439). Standardized in TLS 1.3 and WireGuard VPN.
cipher_desc_twofish: 128-bit block cipher by Bruce Schneier, AES finalist with key-dependent S-boxes.
cipher_desc_blowfish: 64-bit Feistel cipher supporting variable keys up to 448 bits. The core of bcrypt password hashing.
cipher_desc_serpent: AES finalist with 32 rounds of substitution-permutation network for extreme security margins.
cipher_desc_des: Historic standards: DES (56-bit key) and Triple DES (3DES, three-stage EDE processing).
cipher_desc_idea: 128-bit block cipher utilizing mixed algebraic groups. The foundation of original PGP.
cipher_desc_rc: Ron Rivest ciphers: stream cipher RC4, block cipher RC5, and AES finalist RC6.
cipher_desc_camellia_aria: National cryptographic standards: Japanese Camellia (NTT/Mitsubishi) and South Korean ARIA (RFC 5794).
cipher_desc_rsa_ecc: Public-key systems: hybrid RSA-OAEP 2048-bit encryption, ECDSA (P-256) digital signatures, and ECDH key agreement.
cipher_desc_dh: Classical Diffie-Hellman key exchange over discrete logarithm groups (RFC 3526 MODP 2048-bit).
cipher_desc_ml_kem: NIST FIPS 203 Post-Quantum standard (Kyber). Security levels: ML-KEM-512 (Level 1), ML-KEM-768 (Level 3), ML-KEM-1024 (Level 5) using Module-LWE lattices.
cipher_desc_ml_dsa: NIST FIPS 204 Post-Quantum digital signature standard (Dilithium) based on module lattices.
cipher_faq_a1: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is a lattice-based key encapsulation mechanism. A hybrid scheme is used for text: the public key encapsulates an ephemeral secret, which is then used by AES-GCM to encrypt the message securely.
cipher_faq_q2: What is the difference between ML-KEM 512, 768, and 1024?
cipher_faq_a2: The number designates the lattice matrix rank. ML-KEM-512 targets AES-128 equivalent security, ML-KEM-768 matches AES-192 (the recommended default), and ML-KEM-1024 provides maximum post-quantum security matching AES-256.
cipher_faq_q3: Why is a hybrid scheme used for RSA?
cipher_faq_a3: Pure RSA-OAEP 2048 can only encrypt up to 190 bytes at a time. The hybrid scheme uses RSA to encrypt a 256-bit AES session key, which then encrypts messages of any length with AES-GCM.
cipher_faq_q4: How do I verify an ECDSA signature from an external source?
cipher_faq_a4: Enter the message in the input area, paste the hex signature in the 'Digital Signature' field, paste the author's public key in the 'Public Key' field, and click 'Verify Signature'.
cipher_faq_q5: Why does changing any character in the DES key produce garbage?
cipher_faq_a5: All passwords pass through a key derivation function (SHA-256/PBKDF2), ensuring that altering even a single character produces an entirely different key, causing decryption to fail.
cipher_faq_q6: How does key agreement work in ECDH and Diffie-Hellman?
cipher_faq_a6: You generate your keypair and paste your peer's public key in the 'Public Key' field. The algorithm derives the identical shared secret on both ends without transmitting it.
cipher_faq_q7: Can I save generated keys to files?
cipher_faq_a7: Yes, clicking 'Download Public' or 'Download Private' downloads your PEM or hex keys as files directly to your device.
cipher_faq_q8: Is it safe to paste private keys here?
cipher_faq_a8: Yes. All computations run 100% locally in your browser sandbox using Web Crypto API. No keys or plaintexts are ever sent over the network.
cipher_faq_q9: What is the avalanche effect in cryptography?
cipher_faq_a9: It is a crucial property where changing even one bit in the input plaintext or key changes approximately 50% of the output bits pseudo-randomly.

You can inspect the Network tab in DevTools — zero payload bytes leave your machine.
tools_hub_faq_q2: Do these tools work offline without an internet connection?
tools_hub_faq_a2: Yes. Once the web application is loaded in your browser, all cryptographic calculators, encoders, and generators function completely offline.
tools_hub_faq_q3: Are the signatures and ciphertexts standard-compliant?
